title: graceful-degradation-fallback-eviction-arch-review-notes
notes:
Meeting: Architecture review — Graceful degradation, model fallback chains & eviction policy
Date: 2025-02-14
Attendees: Aisha Patel (chair), Evan Chen, Priya Desai, Liam O'Connor, Zhang Wei, Nora Martinez, (observing: Samir Rao)
Duration: 60m

Context / Problem statement:
- Customers running high-concurrency inference see tail-latency spikes when GPU memory is saturated (large KV cache, long-context chat workloads). We need an operable policy for reclaiming memory and degrading work gracefully without breaking correctness for high-SLO customers.
- Current behavior: abrupt OOM kills or broad request throttling. No structured fallback chain.

Goals / Non-goals:
- Goals: 1) ensure high-SLO (enterprise) traffic retains sub-100ms median token latency where possible; 2) provide deterministic, observable fallback chains when full model capacity unavailable; 3) minimize quality regressions for incremental fallback; 4) support safe canary rollouts and per-customer policy.
- Non-goal: re-architect KV storage engine or replace current attention kernel; focus on policy + runtime hooks for eviction/fallback.

Agenda:
1) Quick review of constraints and metrics to monitor
2) Proposed tiered fallback + eviction scoring algorithm
3) Trade-offs and alternatives (A/B/C)
4) Rollout, observability, and testing plan
5) Action items and owners

Key constraints and signals:
- Memory pressure signals: GPU free-memory below 10% (hard), below 20% (soft), per-device fragmentation metrics, and OOM counter increments.
- Request signals: SLO tier (enterprise vs free), request priority, model-version pinned by customer.
- Quality signal: model-comparison delta (embedding similarity + token-level divergence) measured via in-flight canary evals.

Proposal (consensus): Tiered fallback chain + size-weighted, prefix-aware eviction with request-aware prioritization
- Fallback chain per-request: primary model -> quantized-compatible variant (same architecture, lower precision) -> compact small-model fallback (architecturally compatible but fewer params) -> cached-prefix-completion (best-effort reuse of KV prefixes) -> rate-limited degrade (truncate context / fall back to summary).
- Eviction: global score per-KV-entry = alpha * recency_score + beta * size_weight + gamma * prefix_relevance + delta * request_priority_penalty. Default coefficients: alpha=0.5, beta=0.25, gamma=0.15, delta=0.10.
- Soft vs hard eviction: soft eviction marks entries as reclaimable (no immediate removal) and adds them to a background compaction queue. Hard eviction is used only when soft queue cannot free memory in target time window.
- Prefix sensitivity: when prefix hits are high (>30% of tokens), lower eviction score for entries matching active routing prefixes.
- Request-aware prioritization: requests stamped with customer_tier and route_priority influence delta in score so high-tier traffic keeps KV affinity.

Runtimes/hooks required:
- Memory watcher process per-GPU that emits states: OK, SOFT_PRESSURE, HARD_PRESSURE.
- Fallback resolver in request path that consults per-route fallback policy (configurable in Console).
- Eviction planner that runs continuous background compaction and executes hard evictions when required with a bounded rate (e.g., max 4% of KV entries per second to avoid large quality cliffs).
- Telemetry hooks: emit fallback_event (which step chosen), eviction_event (id, size, score, cause), model_switch_event (latency delta, quality delta).

Alternatives considered:
- Alternative A: Global LRU-only eviction (simple). Pros: easy to implement, predictable. Cons: ignores prefix importance and request tiers, can evict high-value entries causing high-quality regressions.
- Alternative B: Per-customer dedicated quotas (strict isolation). Pros: strongest isolation. Cons: higher resource waste, complex cross-customer packing, may increase cost for small customers.
- Alternative C: Aggressive early quantization fallback (force-quantize model instances on memory pressure). Pros: biggest memory wins. Cons: could introduce notable quality regressions; requires validated quantization profiles for every model version.
Decision: choose proposed hybrid (tiered fallback + score-based eviction) because it balances predictability, quality preservation, and implementation effort. Keep option C as a toggled policy for low-SLO tiers where cost savings outweigh quality loss.

Tradeoffs and Risks:
- Risk: Score coefficients require tuning per workload; bad defaults may hurt tail quality. Mitigation: start with conservative coefficients + automated tuning via offline replay traces.
- Risk: Fallback chains increase system complexity and test surface. Mitigation: strict runtime safety checks, circuit breaker on fallback frequency.
- Risk: Observability blind spots for cross-GPU KV references. Mitigation: add span-level tracing for eviction/migration events.

Observability and metrics to add (minimum):
- fallback_rate per-model-per-route, broken down by fallback step
- eviction_rate, eviction_size_distribution, average_eviction_score
- memory_pressure_state transition counts and time-in-state
- model_switch_quality_delta 95/50 quantiles (using canary evals)
- top-20 KV prefixes by read frequency and eviction churn

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (lab): integrate eviction planner & fallback resolver + unit tests (2 weeks)
- Phase 1 (staging canary): enable on staging traffic, replay high-load traces (1 week)
- Phase 2 (production canary): 1% of production requests (low-SLO tenants only) for 72 hours, monitor fallback_rate and quality_delta. Metrics gating: fallback_rate < 5% and avg quality_delta < 0.03 embedding-similarity drop.
- Phase 3 (wider rollout): 10% -> 25% -> 100% over controlled windows.

Testing & validation:
- Offline replay harness with historical traces to simulate memory pressure and record fallback decisions.
- Automated regression suite: synthetic long-context chat, prefix-heavy workloads, and enterprise SLO simulation.
- Add end-to-end QA test that asserts no request-serving OOM after fallback resolver engaged.

Open questions (to be resolved):
- How to dimension alpha/beta/gamma/delta per-model family? (Action: collect model family traces and run tuning job)
- Is there a safe, fast on-GPU compaction primitive we can rely on or do we need to do application-level compaction? (Action: infra spike)
- Should quantized-compatible variants be built and validated for every model by default, or only for top-used models? (Action: product + applied-ml decision)

Action items:

- "Sketch fallback resolver API and route-config UI knobs" — Priya Desai — due 2025-02-20
- "Run offline replay to generate tuning candidates for score coefficients" — Liam O'Connor — due 2025-02-25
- "Infra spike: feasibility of in-place GPU compaction" — Zhang Wei — due 2025-02-22
- "Prepare staging canary plan and metric dashboards" — Nora Martinez — due 2025-02-24

Notes for docs and Console integration:
- Add new Console page: Runtime -> Degradation Policies (perm controls, per-route priorities, fallback chains)
- Document minimum telemetry fields and schema in our observability cookbook for SLO teams.

Next meeting: 2025-02-18 10:00 PT — goal: review prototypes (memory watcher + fallback resolver API) and finalize canary gating thresholds.

End of notes.
